title: René Caillié to Djenné, Timbuktu and Morocco
intro: René Caillié, a Frenchman who had spent months among the Brakna Moors learning Arabic and the customs of Islam, set out alone dressed as a Muslim. He wished to reach Timbuktu and describe it for a prize of 9,000 francs offered by the Société de Géographie in Paris.
ending: Caillié was the first European to return alive from Timbuktu. The Société de Géographie awarded him the prize, and in 1830 its gold medal.

legs.title: From the Rio Nuñez to Djenné

stops.text: Caillié had come by ship from Sierra Leone to Boké on the Rio Nuñez. From Kakondy, near Boké, he set off east along the hills of Fouta Djallon.
stops.quote: Starting from Kakondy near Boké on the Rio Nuñez on 19 April 1827, Caillié travelled east along the hills of Fouta Djallon

stops.text: Beyond the head streams of the Senegal River, Caillié crossed the Upper Niger at Kurussa, now Kouroussa.
stops.quote: passing the head streams of the Senegal River and crossing the Upper Niger at Kurussa (now Kouroussa).

stops.text: He arrived with a caravan carrying kola nuts and stayed a month in this commercial centre. Warned against going north because Kankan was fighting for the Bouré gold area, he left eastwards.
stops.quote: Caillié reached Kankan in present-day Guinea on 17 June 1827 travelling with a caravan transporting kola nuts.

stops.text: In the Kong highlands Caillié was held at the village of Tiémé by illness for five months. He resumed his journey in January 1828 and went north-east.
stops.quote: where at the village of Tiémé in present-day Ivory Coast, he was detained for five months (3 August 1827 – 9 January 1828) by illness.

stops.text: Caillié stayed in Djenné from 11 to 23 March. He confused the Bani River with the Niger, which he called the Dhioliba, and left for Timbuktu on a boat carrying merchandise.
stops.quote: reached the city of Djenné, where he stayed 11–23 March.

stops.text: Caillié arrived by river and stayed about two weeks. He found the city a mass of earth houses, smaller and less busy than he had expected, and less commercial than Djenné.
stops.quote: He arrived in Timbuktu on 20 April 1828.

stops.text: Caillié left Timbuktu on 4 May with a caravan of 600 camels. After six days it reached Araouane, a village that served the trans-Saharan trade. On 19 May it left with 1,400 camels and 400 men.
stops.quote: When the caravan left Araouane on 19 May it included 1,400 camels and 400 men.

stops.text: The caravan carried slaves, gold, ivory, gum, ostrich feathers and cloth across the Sahara. Caillié reached Fez on 12 August.
From Tangier, Caillié returned to France by frigate, landing at Toulon. Back in France he was awarded the prize of 9,000 francs by the Société de Géographie.
stops.quote: From Tangier he returned by frigate to Toulon in France.

notes: Dates not stated are null: Kouroussa and Tangier. The Araouane date is the caravan's departure on 19 May; the arrival (six days after 4 May) is not dated. Caillié's text names Kakondy; wp points at Boké, which the article names beside it. Entry for Fez left null (places.tsv has only Fezzan). Left out: Kouna, Lac Débo, Sa, Mopti/Isaca (named in passing or only as river or lake stages; Sa has no date or event beyond joining a flotilla), Saint-Louis and Sierra Leone (earlier stages, undated). The article's 'a year later' for Timbuktu and the 20 April 1828 date agree. 'By' for Kakondy is sea: he travelled by ship to Boké.
